insights.lesson_learned: When reading runtime-visible annotations from classfile, absence of elements implies use of annotation default; code must explicitly check for that.

insights.title: Adjust close behavior to handle I/O threads and platform differences
insights.problem: Closing a blocking SocketChannel while I/O operations are in progress had platform-specific semantics that produced resets on Windows.
insights.root_cause: Close logic didn't account for presence (or absence) of tracked I/O operations and platform-specific handling for virtual vs platform threads.
insights.solution: Enhanced implCloseBlockingMode javadoc and logic to call shutdown output when Net.shouldShutdownWriteBeforeClose() indicates so; adjusted the ordering of preClose and tryClose to ensure proper shutdown when required.
insights.lesson_learned: I/O close semantics must handle multiple thread types (virtual, platform) and platform differences; prefer explicit platform checks and guard conditions.

insights.title: Avoid NPE / crash in javap when encountering preview classfile minor version
insights.problem: javap crashed (NPE) for class files with preview minor version numbers because the code returned null in cffv() for unsupported combinations.
insights.root_cause: candidates returned null for non-representable ClassFileFormatVersion; code later dereferenced or assumed non-null.
insights.solution: Return ClassFileFormatVersion.latest() as a safe fallback when major/minor combos are not representable rather than returning null — ensures javap can handle preview/minor combos gracefully.
insights.lesson_learned: Tools that inspect class files should be tolerant of preview/minor version encodings and prefer a best-effort fallback rather than null which can cause downstream NPE/crash.

insights.title: Compute reg-save area size from centralized helper and align when vector registers used
insights.problem: Upcall stub generation used old logic to compute callee-saved area; with new vector register saving logic we need centralized size computation and alignment.
insights.root_cause: Changes to non-volatile register saving required callers that allocate frame space to be updated to use new size routines and alignment for VSX registers.
insights.solution: Use MacroAssembler::__ save_nonvolatile_registers_size(true, SuperwordUseVSX) and align reg_save_area_offset accordingly.
insights.lesson_learned: When low-level ABI frame layout changes, every stub/assembler site that computes frame sizes must be updated to use centralized helpers to avoid mismatch.

insights.title: Introduce VM_Version::VM_Features top-level type and bitmap fields
insights.problem: Representation of CPU feature flags was a single uint64_t bitmask; new AVX10 feature indices exceed 64 bits and require a bitmap.
insights.root_cause: Adding many features (AVX10 versions) made single 64-bit mask insufficient.
insights.solution: Add VM_Features as a toplevel type, static field _features, and nonstatic field _features_bitmap[0] plus size, adjust VM_STRUCTS entries.
insights.lesson_learned: When extending enum-like feature sets beyond existing bit capacity, migrate to a bitmap data structure and update all consumers (VM structs, JVMCI) carefully.

insights.title: Support AVX10 detection and feature bitmap management
insights.problem: New Intel AVX10 converged ISA needs detection and representation.
insights.root_cause: Existing VM feature flags were single-bit indexes in a 64-bit mask; AVX10 introduces versioned flags that require indexing and a bitmap.
insights.solution: Added new Feature_Flag entries (AVX10_1, AVX10_2), introduced VM_Features class encapsulating bitmap operations, added _features and _cpu_features VM_Features instances, changed feature accessor APIs to use _features.supports_feature(...), and added helper methods and offsets.
insights.lesson_learned: Encapsulate feature-bit operations in a VM_Features class to make adding future features easier and avoid scattering bit-manipulation logic.

insights.title: Compute MASK_THROTTLE* constants as long to avoid shift truncation
insights.problem: MASK_THROTTLE and MASK_THROTTLE_CHECK were computed as int shifts (1 << 62/63) leading to incorrect signed/overflow behavior and wrong masks.
insights.root_cause: Using int literal 1 with large shift produced undefined/truncated/miscomputed masks instead of long constants.
insights.solution: Change magic constants to use 1L so that the shifts produce long values: 1L << 62 and 1L << 63.
insights.lesson_learned: Bit masks beyond 31 bits must be computed using proper-width integer literal (1L) to avoid integer overflow and platform-dependent behavior.

insights.title: Bytecode instrumentation updated for throttling: duration bitmasking and trampoline
insights.problem: Instrumented event classes need to store throttle information in the duration field and ensure throttle checks are performed correctly in generated 'shouldCommit' logic.
insights.root_cause: Introduction of event throttling requires preserving throttle bit(s) and performing extra calls to eventConfiguration.throttle(...) which returns duration with throttle bits encoded; instrumentation must honor that.
insights.solution: Add MASK_THROTTLE, MASK_THROTTLE_CHECK, helper methods getDuration/setDuration that mask/unmask throttle bits, add code to call eventConfiguration.throttle(...) and check throttle mask in methodShouldCommit generation. Add support for different overloads of shouldThrottleCommit in static/untyped contexts.
insights.lesson_learned: When adding metadata-driven runtime transformations (throttle bits encoded into existing fields), implement helper methods to encapsulate masking/unmasking and update all instrumentation generation paths to maintain compatibility and correctness.

insights.title: SEALED/NON_SEALED flag collisions and ExtendedStandardFlags overlay mistake
insights.problem: Flags used for multiple Symbol kinds overlapped/changed causing misleading compile-time errors such as 'sealed is not allowed here'.
insights.root_cause: A SEALED flag was previously defined with a Symbol-kind specific usage (different bit for ClassSymbols) and ExtendedStandardFlags contained bits that could be reused/overlaid across symbol kinds, producing incorrect diagnostics when bits had different meanings depending on symbol kind.
insights.solution: Consolidated SEALED/NON_SEALED into bits that are part of ExtendedStandardFlags and annotated comments to mark they cannot be reused; removed duplicate SEALED definition for ClassSymbols and added SEALED into the Flags enum in the correct position. Also ensured ExtendedStandardFlags is declared so overlaying across Symbol kinds is not allowed.
insights.lesson_learned: Bit flags that are shared at different symbol kinds must not be overlayed; keep a central authoritative definition for flags used in multiple symbol kinds and document when bits are reserved (ExtendedStandardFlags).

insights.title: Replace direct duration calculation and emit with offer API for socket events
insights.problem: Socket instrumentation previously computed duration and called emit() when shouldCommit returned true; that logic is now encapsulated in SocketReadEvent.offer / SocketWriteEvent.offer.
insights.root_cause: JFR throttling and commit API changed to use offer helpers which compute duration and decide commit via generated throttle checks.
insights.solution: Replace manual duration computation and conditional emit with SocketReadEvent.offer(start, nbytes, remote, timeout) and SocketWriteEvent.offer(start, len, remote).
insights.lesson_learned: Framework-level event sampling changes require sweeping updates to all instrumentation points to use the new helpers. Search for shouldCommit/emit usage patterns when migrating.

insights.title: Platform-specific shutdown-write-before-close heuristic
insights.problem: On Windows, closing a SocketChannel while a thread is blocked reading caused a connection reset rather than a graceful EOF due to differing platform semantics.
insights.root_cause: No platform-specific decision to call shutdown(SHUT_WR) before close; behavior must differ between Unix and Windows.
insights.solution: Added SHUTDOWN_WRITE_BEFORE_CLOSE StableValue and shouldShutdownWriteBeforeClose() native hook to decide per-platform whether to shutdown write before close; used in SocketChannelImpl implCloseBlockingMode logic.
insights.lesson_learned: Socket closing semantics differ across platforms; encapsulate heuristics in platform hooks and document behavior.

insights.title: Fix KeyInfo check for MAC initialization with unknown key algorithms
insights.problem: P11SecretKeyFactory rejected using keys with unrecognized algorithms for HMAC/MAC services even though any key may be used to initialize Mac instances (for SHA-based HMACs).
insights.root_cause: Logic checked keyInfo based on key algorithm too early and did not special-case HMAC properly.
insights.solution: Skip KeyInfo.checkUse for HMAC (HMACKeyInfo) cases and defer retrieval/validation of KeyInfo for keyAlgo only when needed. Ensure PBEKey checks still use appropriate KeyInfo.
insights.lesson_learned: Crypto API initializers must account for algorithm-specific semantics (e.g., HMACs accept any secret key material) and avoid strict algorithm-name-based checks that reject valid keys.

src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.short_description: JFR setting that accepts method filter strings and triggers PlatformTracer initialization and filter application
src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.description:
MethodSetting is a Java Flight Recorder (JFR) configuration setting representing method-based filters used by MethodTrace/MethodTiming features. It exists to expose a user-configurable text-based filter for methods, validate that text, and apply the filter to the runtime tracing subsystem. The class extends FilterSetting (not provided here) and delegates validation to Filter.isValid and application of filters to PlatformTracer.setFilters.

Design-wise, MethodSetting intentionally performs lazy, once-only initialization of the heavy PlatformTracer subsystem: it holds a volatile static boolean initialized and a private ensureInitialized() method that calls PlatformTracer.initialize() exactly once (and then sets the flag). The code documents that ensureInitialized is expected to be called while holding an external lock so no extra internal synchronization is used. MethodSetting also exposes a public isInitialized accessor used by tests or other code to query whether initialization has happened. This class is part of the JFR internal settings package and serves as the bridge between user settings and the low-level tracing internals implemented in PlatformTracer.

key_constructs.reasoning: When a user changes the filter setting for MethodTrace/MethodTiming, the runtime needs a lightweight setting object to validate the text and then propagate the resulting filters to PlatformTracer. MethodSetting encapsulates that behavior, avoids unnecessary eager initialization, and records whether initialization has occurred.

src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.short_description: Core implementation of method-level tracing/timing support and management of filters, timed classes/methods and initialization
src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.description:
PlatformTracer implements the low-level runtime support for method tracing and timing used by JFR's MethodTrace and MethodTiming facilities. It centralizes management of timed classes and methods (timedClasses, timedMethods), applies textual filters to the JVM (via JVM.setMethodTraceFilters), and contains the expensive initialize() routine that warms up and exports the tracing package to other modules. The class also provides the entry point onMethodTrace(...) used by the JVM to request bytecode instrumentation for matching methods.

The design isolates the tracing implementation within an internal package so only the JFR internals use it (the jdk.jfr.tracing package is exported to other modules selectively). PlatformTracer uses concurrent collections to store method/timing state and performs several native interactions: calling JVM.setMethodTraceFilters and JVM.drainStaleMethodTracerIds, and generating bytecode through Instrumentation. initialize() intentionally performs several side effects (excludes the current thread from instrumentation, loads class bytes from resources, calls onMethodTrace to generate instrumentation, exercises MethodTracer API heavily to warm up, resets internal maps, includes current thread back, and calls SecuritySupport.addTracingExport to export modules). Logging is used extensively to report progress and errors. The class also exposes utility operations to add timings, publish classes (publishClass), and to clear internal state (reset).

key_constructs.name: PlatformTracer
key_constructs.purpose: Provides the runtime implementation for method tracing/timing, filter management, and initialization
key_constructs.reasoning: Centralizes the stateful and native interactions required to support JFR method tracing/timing features. Any edits must preserve the concurrency, JVM interactions, and initialization side-effects.

key_constructs.name: onMethodTrace
key_constructs.purpose: Called by the JVM to instrument bytecode; builds Instrumentation for a class and returns modified bytecode if changed
key_constructs.reasoning: This is a hot path invoked during class load/instrumentation; it must be robust to Recursion/Errors and avoid classloader recursion by checking an ExcludeList. It must not throw; instead it logs and returns null when it cannot instrument.

key_constructs.name: initialize
key_constructs.purpose: One-time warmup and export routine that prepares PlatformTracer for live tracing
key_constructs.reasoning: initialize has multiple security and runtime side-effects: it excludes/includes current thread from instrumentation, loads raw class bytes, invokes onMethodTrace to generate bytecode, calls MethodTracer APIs to warm internal counters, resets maps, and calls SecuritySupport.addTracingExport(). The method is expensive and must be invoked only once per JVM as intended.

key_constructs.name: setFilters
key_constructs.purpose: Convert textual filters into runtime Filter objects and publish classes affected by the filters
key_constructs.reasoning: setFilters coordinates the conversion from user settings to native JVM filter state via applyFilter. It then publishes classes returned by the JVM (class ids) so the runtime can begin instrumentation on those classes.

key_constructs.name: applyFilter
key_constructs.purpose: Create Filter objects, update trace/timing filter lists, and call JVM.setMethodTraceFilters; returns class ids to publish
key_constructs.reasoning: This function is the bridge from in-Java Filter representations to the native JVM filtering mechanism. It constructs arrays for native calls using Bytecode helpers and interprets the returned class ids for publishing.

key_constructs.name: emitTiming
key_constructs.purpose: Emit timing events for all timed classes by draining stale classes and iterating timedClasses to emit events
key_constructs.reasoning: emitTiming must hold the MetadataRepository lock while emitting to prevent rotations/flush races; it also drains stale IDs via JVM.drainStaleMethodTracerIds and then asks each TimedClass to emit.

key_constructs.name: addTiming
key_constructs.purpose: Record a duration for a method id by updating the corresponding TimedMethod's counters and min/max
key_constructs.reasoning: This method is invoked when a traced/timed method completes. It must handle the case where the id is not present (method unloaded/removed) and must update aggregates atomically.

key_constructs.name: reset
key_constructs.purpose: Clear internal timedMethods and timedClasses maps
key_constructs.reasoning: Used by initialize() and potentially tests; it must be used cautiously because it drops all runtime timing state.

maintain runtime tables of timed classes and methods
apply user-provided filters to the JVM and publish affected classes
provide a once-only initialize path that warms the subsystem and exports the tracing package

pitfalls.mistake: Calling initialize() repeatedly or from many threads
pitfalls.consequence: initialize is expensive and performs class/resource loading and security exports; repeated calls waste CPU, may race with exports, and can hide failures due to internal exception swallowing
pitfalls.prevention: Only call initialize() once via a lightweight guard in the consumer (e.g. MethodSetting.ensureInitialized). If tests need to call initialize, coordinate with reset/clear internal state as required.

pitfalls.mistake: Assuming initialize() throws on failure
pitfalls.consequence: initialize() catches Exception and logs a WARN; callers will not see an exception. Code that relies on successful initialization should not assume an exception is thrown.
pitfalls.prevention: Check observable side-effects (e.g. expected filters published, SecuritySupport exports) or use tests that assert behavior rather than exception propagation.

pitfalls.mistake: Modifying JVM native interactions (JVM.setMethodTraceFilters / drainStaleMethodTracerIds) without considering JNI/native contract
pitfalls.consequence: Mismatch between Java-side arrays/order and native expectations can produce incorrect classIds or runtime crashes
pitfalls.prevention: When editing applyFilter or related array building code, ensure the order and format match native expectations (classes[], methods[], annotations[], modifications[]).

pitfalls.mistake: Assuming resource stream for java/lang/String.class is always available
pitfalls.consequence: getResourceAsStream could return null in non-standard class loader setups; initialize() assumes it exists and calls readAllBytes() and close() without null checks, which would throw NPE
pitfalls.prevention: Be aware initialize() has implicit assumptions about classloader resources; tests or platform changes that alter resource availability may make initialize() fail and get caught internally.

pitfalls.mistake: Altering logging or SecuritySupport.addTracingExport side-effects lightly
pitfalls.consequence: These are important for diagnosing startup and for module export security policy; removing or moving them can change visibility of the jdk.jfr.tracing package or obscure failures
pitfalls.prevention: Preserve logging and export calls' ordering and semantics unless coordinating with the security module and test updates.

src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.short_description: Manages per-event runtime controls and settings for JFR PlatformEventType instances
src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.description:
EventControl is an internal JFR (Java Flight Recorder) runtime helper that creates and manages SettingControl instances and named controls for a PlatformEventType. Its purpose is to translate annotations and metadata on event types and event Java classes into runtime controls (Enabled, Threshold, StackTrace, Period, Cutoff, Throttle, Level, filter, and user-defined settings). It registers descriptors with the platform metadata (via PrivateAccess) and keeps lists of created SettingControl objects and named Control wrappers.

The class is designed to avoid hard references from PlatformEventType to long-lived SettingControl instances that would prevent proper unloading of event classes. It uses reflection heavily to instantiate user-provided SettingControl implementations, uses module-read manipulation (Modules.addReads) to ensure accessibility between modules, and enforces a particular lifecycle for controls (creation, default-value setting, storing for potential cleanup). It also parses @StackFrameFilter-like annotations, validates class and method identifiers, registers stack filters into a MetadataRepository, and writes ActiveSettingEvent entries reflecting current settings.

EventControl sits at the intersection of JFR metadata (PlatformEventType, Type/TypeLibrary, AnnotationElement), runtime settings (setting descriptors, SettingControl implementations), and runtime behavior (throttling via Throttler, stack filters registration). It is internal to jdk.jfr, not part of the public API surface, and interacts with other internal helpers such as PrivateAccess, TypeLibrary, MetadataRepository, SecuritySupport, Modules, and Logger. Because it creates and keeps SettingControl instances, care is taken to allow class unloading and to avoid leaking resources, as hinted by the class header comment.

src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.short_description: Represents JFR event metadata and runtime controls for platform (JDK/JVM) events
src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.description:
PlatformEventType is an internal JFR (Java Flight Recorder) representation of an event type that holds metadata and runtime control flags for events defined by the JVM and the JDK. It exists to centralize per-event configuration (enabled/disabled, thresholds, periods, throttling, stack-trace handling, instrumentation flags, registration state) and to translate those high-level settings into calls to native/JVM subsystems (via JVMSupport/JVM) when appropriate. The class intentionally avoids holding strong references to event classes or setting classes (see file header) to prevent memory leaks in long-running JVMs — it keeps only descriptors and primitive/POJO fields.

The design separates static description data (name, id, whether event is JDK/JVM, default flags) from dynamic runtime controls. It stores a small list of SettingDescriptor objects and supports a dynamicSettings mode where getSettings filters them based on visibility (Utils.isSettingVisible) and whether an event hook is present. For system-level events (isJVM or isJDK true), changes are propagated into native components: enabling/disabling, threshold conversion to ticks, method-sampling periods and CPU-rate/period changes are all forwarded to JVM or JVMSupport helper methods.

PlatformEventType is tightly coupled to other JFR internals: Type (superclass) for common type metadata, JVMSupport/JVM for native interactions, PeriodicEvents to signal scheduler changes, MetadataRepository when types are unregistered, Logger/LogTag/LogLevel for state logs, and Throttler/TimespanRate for throttling and CPU-rate controls. Many boolean fields act as cached state used for quick checks (e.g., committable caches enabled && registered), and some behavior depends on the event name (determineMethodSampling, getModification, determineStackTraceOffset). Because it operates at the intersection of Java metadata and native runtime configuration, edits must preserve side-effect ordering and the expectations about when native calls are made.

src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.short_description: Java-side JVM/JFR native interface: exposes JFR/VM operations to the jdk.jfr Java layer
src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.description:
This file defines an internal Java façade (final class JVM) that exposes a large set of native operations used by the Java Flight Recorder (JFR) implementation. It exists so the Java code inside the jdk.jfr module can call into VM/native functionality (recording lifecycle, event emission, configuration, sampling, logging and repository management) through a stable Java API. The class groups lifecycle operations (create/destroy JFR, begin/end recording), configuration setters (buffer sizes, stack depth, sampling parameters, file paths), event/metadata operations (getClassId/getTypeId/getStackTraceId/getEventWriter/commit/flush), and logging and subscription APIs that originate in the JVM.

The design is intentionally a thin native bridge: almost every public method is native and often annotated with @IntrinsicCandidate for fast-path mapping to VM intrinsics. The static initializer registers native methods and subscribes log tags, and also triggers Options.ensureInitialized() which establishes Java-side configuration required by JFR. Several native methods throw or declare exceptions (IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException) to indicate JVM-side validation. Some methods are synchronized (retransformClasses) to guard JVMTI/retransform semantics. The class also exposes a CHUNK_ROTATION_MONITOR (HiddenWait) object used for JVM-to-Java synchronization on chunk rotation. Overall, this file is authoritative for the Java-facing signatures of JFR's native contract and must remain consistent with the native side and any VM intrinsics.

Because it is a native contract boundary, changes here impact JNI/native implementations and VM intrinsics. Any edit that changes method names, parameter lists, return types, checked exceptions, or threading/synchronization semantics risks breaking native registration, JNI symbol resolution, or runtime optimizations. The static fields and initializer ordering (registerNatives() then log tag subscriptions and Options initialization) are meaningful: native registration must happen early and Options must be initialized after subscription. The file is central to JFR functionality and coordinates with other jdk.jfr internal classes (EventWriter, LogTag, Options, EventConfiguration) and the native/HotSpot implementation of JFR.

pitfalls.mistake: Rename or change signature of any native method (name, params, return type, checked exceptions).
pitfalls.consequence: Native method registration and JNI/native implementations will fail to bind; runtime errors or NoSuchMethodError and broken JFR functionality will result.
pitfalls.prevention: Preserve exact method names, parameter types and declared exceptions; coordinate any change with corresponding native/JVM code and registerNatives mapping.

pitfalls.mistake: Remove or reorder the static initialization logic (registerNatives and log tag subscription).
pitfalls.consequence: Native registration may not happen or may happen too late; log subscriptions and Options initialization might be inconsistent leading to initialization-time races or missed subscriptions.
pitfalls.prevention: Keep static initializer semantics and ordering intact; if changing, ensure equivalent native registration and Options initialization occur before other code depends on JFR.

pitfalls.mistake: Modify CHUNK_ROTATION_MONITOR type/identity or replace HiddenWait with a plain Object.
pitfalls.consequence: Native code expecting HiddenWait behavior or identity-based synchronization may malfunction; chunk rotation notifications could deadlock or be missed.
pitfalls.prevention: Retain CHUNK_ROTATION_MONITOR as a static final HiddenWait and avoid altering its semantics without corresponding native changes.

pitfalls.mistake: Change methods annotated with @IntrinsicCandidate (e.g., counterTime, commit, getEventWriter) without coordinating VM intrinsics.
pitfalls.consequence: Loss of intrinsic/fast-path performance or incorrect intrinsic binding; could break JFR hot paths and degrade performance.
pitfalls.prevention: Any change to intrinsic candidates must be synchronized with VM intrinsics and native code changes; treat these methods as performance-sensitive contract points.

pitfalls.mistake: Remove synchronized modifier from retransformClasses.
pitfalls.consequence: Concurrent retransform requests may violate JVMTI phase requirements causing IllegalStateException or undefined native-state behavior.
pitfalls.prevention: Preserve synchronization semantics or ensure an equivalent concurrency protocol in both Java and native code.

src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/events.short_description: JFR event type describing per-method timing statistics (min/avg/max/invocations).
src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/events.description:
This file declares a Java Flight Recorder (JFR) event class named MethodTimingEvent. It exists to define the shape and metadata of an event that records approximate execution-time statistics for a method: the number of invocations and the minimum, average and maximum observed times. The class is annotated with JFR-specific annotations (Name, Label, Category, Timespan, Description, RemoveFields) that are used by the JFR tooling and event generator to produce event metadata and wiring. The static stub methods (commit, timestamp, enabled) are placeholders expected to be replaced/implemented/generated by JFR tooling at build/runtime.

This class is part of the jdk.jfr module and is used by the JVM/JFR recorder to emit aggregated timing events for methods. The fields use primitive long types and Timespan(Timespan.TICKS) for timing values; the field Descriptions document sentinel behavior (Long.MIN_VALUE) used when values cannot be established (e.g., clock resolution issues). RemoveFields lists fields (duration, eventThread, stackTrace) that are intentionally omitted from this event's metadata; altering those annotations changes the recorded metadata and how tools interpret the event. Because this is an event shape consumed by tools and tooling (and potentially by external analyzers), field names, types, and annotations are part of the event's public metadata surface and must be respected by any changes.

src/java.base/share/classes/jdk/internal.short_description: Java-side representation of a thread snapshot populated by the VM for inspection and tooling.
src/java.base/share/classes/jdk/internal.description:
ThreadSnapshot is a package-private Java class that models a snapshot of a Thread's runtime state as filled in by the VM. It exists as the Java-side mirror of VM-provided data used by internal tooling and diagnostics (thread dumps, jcmd/jstack-like features, monitoring). The VM populates the private fields of an instance (via the native create(Thread) method) and ThreadSnapshot.of(Thread) is the factory that converts the VM-provided raw values into runtime-friendly Java constructs (e.g., mapping ordinals to enums, converting blocker object into a ThreadBlocker record, finishing initialization of ThreadLock entries).

Design-wise, the class keeps a thin layer between raw VM fields (primitive/objects filled from native code) and the idiomatic Java API exposed to callers in the jdk.internal.vm package: threadName(), threadState(), stackTrace(), ownsMonitors(), ownedMonitorsAt(), blockedOn(), waitingOn(), parkBlocker(), and carrierThread(). Nested types capture lock and blocker information: ThreadLock (now static), OwnedLockType, BlockerLockType, and ThreadBlocker record. ordinals from the VM are converted into enums via cached arrays to avoid repeated lookup. The class explicitly manages nulls for stackTrace and locks (replaces with EMPTY_* constants) and clears the reference to blockerObject after constructing a ThreadBlocker to avoid retaining object references beyond necessary.

This file tightly couples to native VM code: the private fields are populated by a native method (create), and ordinals used to encode enum values must match the VM's expectations. The class is not part of the public JDK API; it is internal and used by internal tooling and tests. Historical commit notes indicate (1) of() was changed to return null when the native create returned null (to model thread termination gracefully) and (2) ThreadLock was made static to avoid implicit enclosing-instance retention. Those historical facts are important to preserve behavior and ABI contract with the VM.

pitfalls.mistake: Renaming, retyping, or reordering the private fields that the native create(Thread) populates.
pitfalls.consequence: Native VM implementation will not be able to find/populate fields correctly — causing runtime failures, incorrect snapshots, or JVM crashes.
pitfalls.prevention: Preserve field names, types and intended null/empty semantics; coordinate with native VM changes before editing these fields.

pitfalls.mistake: Changing enum values, their order, or their ordinal-based mapping logic (e.g., altering BlockerLockType/OwnedLockType order or removing cached value arrays).
pitfalls.consequence: Ordinal-to-enum mapping between VM and Java will diverge; blocker/lock types will be misinterpreted leading to incorrect diagnostics/behavior.
pitfalls.prevention: Maintain ordinal stability and the mapping pattern (cached values arrays) or ensure corresponding native-side updates are made in lockstep.

pitfalls.mistake: Converting ThreadLock back to a non-static inner class or adding references from ThreadLock instances to the enclosing ThreadSnapshot.
pitfalls.consequence: Unintended retention of the outer instance leading to increased memory usage and possibly retaining references the VM expects to be released.
pitfalls.prevention: Keep ThreadLock static unless there's a deliberate and coordinated native+Java change explaining why an outer reference is required.

pitfalls.mistake: Removing the step that nulls blockerObject after constructing ThreadBlocker (release of reference).
pitfalls.consequence: Retaining blockerObject on the snapshot longer than intended might prevent garbage collection of objects that should be eligible sooner.
pitfalls.prevention: Retain current behavior where the raw blockerObject is nulled once converted to ThreadBlocker.

insights.title: ThreadSnapshot.of returns null when snapshot not created instead of throwing
insights.problem: Previously create(thread) returning null resulted in an exception being thrown by of(); that made callers assume snapshot always present.
insights.root_cause: API contract change to allow of() to return null when thread terminated; callers must handle null.
insights.solution: Modify of() to return null (instead of throwing) if snapshot creation failed/returned null. Document behavior.
insights.lesson_learned: API design: prefer returning null for 'not available' where callers can cope versus throwing exceptions that complicate normal control flow; ensure callers updated accordingly.

insights.title: Make ThreadLock a static nested class
insights.problem: ThreadLock nested as non-static inner class captured an implicit reference to the enclosing ThreadSnapshot instance unnecessarily.
insights.root_cause: No use of the outer instance inside ThreadLock, making the implicit reference redundant and potentially increasing memory retention.
insights.solution: Change 'private class ThreadLock' to 'private static class ThreadLock'.
insights.lesson_learned: Prefer static nested classes when the inner class does not need an implicit reference to the outer instance — avoids accidental memory retention and is clearer about independence.

src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.short_description: JFR setting control that parses, combines, and applies CPU-sample emission rate limits.
src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.description:
This class represents a Java Flight Recorder (JFR) setting that upper-bounds the emission rate for CPU time samples. It exists to expose a configurable rate (expressed as a TimespanRate string like "X/s") for a PlatformEventType that produces CPU samples, to combine multiple setting inputs into a single effective rate, and to apply that rate to the underlying PlatformEventType. The class is annotated with JFR metadata annotations (@MetadataDefinition, @Label, @Description, @Name) so it participates in JFR settings discovery and management. It lives in an internal package (jdk.jfr.internal.settings) and subclasses SettingControl, meaning it's part of the JFR settings framework rather than a general public API.

Design-wise, the class stores the currently effective value as a String (initialized to DEFAULT_VALUE = "0/s") and keeps a final reference to the associated PlatformEventType provided at construction. The combine(Set<String>) method interprets multiple input strings by parsing them into TimespanRate objects and selecting the one with the highest resolution (via TimespanRate.selectHigherResolution). The setValue(String) method parses a single string into a TimespanRate and, if valid, calls eventType.setCPUThrottle(rate) and updates the stored string value; invalid strings are ignored silently. getValue simply returns the last stored string value. The class uses Objects.requireNonNull for the PlatformEventType in the constructor.

This file is small but sits at an integration point between: (a) the JFR settings system (SettingControl and the metadata annotations), (b) the TimespanRate parsing/selection utilities, and (c) PlatformEventType which actually applies the throttle. Any edits must respect those contracts: annotations for metadata discovery, the string representation used for persistence/display, the parsing semantics of TimespanRate, and the side-effect on PlatformEventType. There are non-obvious behaviors (see Pitfalls) that an edit agent must be careful with when changing combination, parsing, or storage logic.

src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.short_description: Represents a JFR timespan or rate setting and provides parsing/formatting and resolution selection.
src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.description:
TimespanRate is a small immutable value type (a Java record) used by the JFR internals to represent either a fixed time period (in nanoseconds) or an event rate (per second). This type exists because JFR configuration supports both kinds of specifications (explicit time periods such as "1ms" and rates such as "10/s"), plus a special "off" value. The record stores three pieces of data: a double rate (events per second), a long periodNanos, and a boolean isRate that denotes which interpretation is active.

The class supplies parsing (of textual settings), formatting (toString that emits a normalized textual representation), and a helper to pick the higher-resolution representation when two TimespanRate values must be reconciled. Parsing delegates to ValueParser.parseTimespanWithInfinity for timespans and to Rate.of for rate strings. selectHigherResolution contains the logic that, given two TimespanRate values, decides which has higher sampling resolution — if both are rates it picks the larger rate, if both are periods it picks the shorter period, and if mixed it converts the period to an equivalent rate using Runtime.availableProcessors() and converts to a rate TimespanRate (isRate=true).

This file is part of the JFR internal utilities; it's small but central to interpreting and normalizing JFR setting strings, and it interacts with other utilities: Rate (parsing/representing rates), ValueParser (parsing time spans including special infinity handling), and TimespanUnit (units used for formatting). It is used where JFR settings need canonical values (for validation, UI or persistence) and where multiple settings need to be reconciled for effective sampling resolution.

test/lib/jdk/test/lib/jfr/EventNames.jav.short_description: Centralized constants and helper for JDK-shipped JFR event name identifiers used by tests.
test/lib/jdk/test/lib/jfr/EventNames.jav.description:
This file is a small test-library utility that centralizes the canonical string identifiers for Java Flight Recorder (JFR) events that are shipped with the JDK. It exists to give JDK test code a single authoritative place to import event name constants from, avoiding hard-coded strings scattered across tests and making tests easier to read and maintain. The class groups event name constants by subsystem (JVM configuration, runtime, GC, compiler, OS, JDK, containers, Flight Recorder, diagnostics) which mirrors the taxonomy used by the JFR implementation.

Beyond constants, the class provides a single helper method, isGcEvent(EventType), which determines whether an EventType belongs to the GC category by checking its category names. Tests that need to detect or filter GC-related events should use this helper instead of repeating the category check logic. The file is placed under test/lib so it is not part of the JDK runtime, but is bundled with the test harness (jtreg / test frameworks) and intended to be referenced by many JFR-related tests across the test suite.

Because tests rely on exact event id strings, this file effectively bridges test expectations and the event ids defined in the platform. Any edits must preserve those semantics: the string constants must match the event ids used by the runtime's JFR event definitions, and the isGcEvent logic must remain compatible with how EventType exposes category names at runtime.

src/java.base/share/classes/java/util/Lo.short_description: Core Locale implementation representing language, script, region, variant, and extensions (BCP 47/LDML aware).
src/java.base/share/classes/java/util/Lo.description:
This is the JDK's canonical java.util.Locale implementation. It encodes locale identity (language, script, region/country, variant and extensions) and implements parsing/formatting behavior and matching algorithms compatible with IETF BCP 47 (RFC 5646/4647) with additional support for LDML/UTS#35 Unicode locale extension semantics. The class exists to provide the platform-wide representation of locales used by all locale-sensitive APIs (java.text, java.time formatters, resource bundle lookups, NumberFormat, DateFormat, etc.), to enforce canonicalization rules (case normalization for language/script/region, normalization of extension keys/values), and to offer factory and builder APIs for constructing Locale instances in a backward-compatible manner.

The implementation integrates with internal locale infrastructure (sun.util.locale.* and java.util.spi providers) and uses internal JDK utilities (jdk.internal.util.ReferencedKeyMap, StaticProperty, LocaleProviderAdapter and provider pools) for caching and provider lookup. It contains many public API entry points: constants (e.g., UNICODE_LOCALE_EXTENSION), factory methods (forLanguageTag, of, Builder), nested helper types (Locale.Builder, Locale.LanguageRange and Locale.Category), default-locale management (getDefault/setDefault and category-specific variants), display-name APIs (getDisplayLanguage/Country/Script/Variant/Name), Unicode extension accessors (getUnicodeLocaleAttributes, getUnicodeLocaleKeys, getUnicodeLocaleType), matching/filtering algorithms (filter/lookup for RFC 4647), serialization behavior (custom writeObject/readObject/readResolve handling), and conversion between Locale and BCP 47 language tags (toLanguageTag, forLanguageTag).

Because Locale is part of the public Java SE API and has historical behavior to preserve, the class retains compatibility with older constructor semantics (including deprecated constructors) and preserves behavior for toString() and factory overloads that may allow non-BCP-47 inputs. The file also documents and implements subtle compatibility special-cases (for example, special-case handling during deserialization for historical locales such as th_TH_TH and ja_JP_JP). It interacts closely with locale providers and resource lookups — changes here can affect resource bundle selection, locale matching, and all locale-sensitive services across the JDK and applications.

src/java.base/share/classes/sun/security.short_description: Utility for parsing and producing PEM-format blocks (RFC 1421/7468) used by JDK security code
src/java.base/share/classes/sun/security.description:
This class centralizes PEM (Privacy Enhanced Mail) handling used by internal JDK security components. It provides parsing of PEM blocks from an InputStream (readPEM), base64 decoding of PEM payloads (decode), mapping of historical PEM type names to canonical names (typeConverter), determination of PBE algorithm OIDs (getPBEID), and functions to produce PEM-formatted Strings (pemEncoded overloads). It exists to provide consistent PEM semantics for certificate, key and CRL handling across JDK internals (for example, certificate/key loading code and CertificateFactory implementations). The implementation follows RFC 7468 and RFC 1421 conventions (header/footer markers, CRLF line endings, whitespace handling, and historical type normalization).

Design choices evident in the code: stream-based parsing that advances the InputStream to the end-of-block so subsequent reads can continue correctly; returning a java.security.PEMRecord with type, base64 content string and any leading pre-data captured before the PEM header; strict header/footer validation and explicit error reporting by throwing EOFException or IOException for malformed inputs; using Security.getProperty to obtain a default algorithm name (DEFAULT_ALGO) and a regex to detect PBE style algorithm names. The class is package-private in sun.security.util package and is intended to be used by other internal security components rather than public API consumers.

src/jdk.hotspot.agent/share/classes/sun/.short_description: Serviceability Agent helper that reads archived CDS file-map data and maps copied vtable addresses to HotSpot metadata Types
src/jdk.hotspot.agent/share/classes/sun/.description:
This file is part of the Serviceability Agent (SA) side of the HotSpot project (jdk.hotspot.agent). Its purpose is to locate and interpret the FileMap (CDS/Archive) header structures in a target VM image and expose utilities used to reason about copied/cloned C++ vtables that are archived into a mapped region. The class reads low-level metadata from the TypeDataBase and VMObject instances (addresses, offsets, sizes) and builds an in-memory mapping from the addresses of cloned vtables in the archive's RW region to the corresponding HotSpot Type objects (for example, ConstantPool, InstanceKlass, Method, etc.). This mapping is used when the SA inspects archived objects and needs to infer their Java-level metadata type from their (C++) vtable pointer.

Design decisions visible in the file: this is a VM-initialization-driven component — initialization is deferred until the VM has been registered and the TypeDataBase is available via a VMInitialized Observer. Core responsibilities are split between a top-level FileMapInfo class (static helpers, top-level fields) and an inner FileMapHeader class (VMObject wrapper for the FileMapHeader address and operations on it). The code uses low-level abstractions provided by the SA (Address, VMObjectFactory, Type, TypeDataBase, CIntegerField/AddressField) rather than JNI or reflection. It assumes a particular layout for the archived vtable index and the CppVtableInfo structure and that a fixed list of metadata Type names represent the archived metadata types.

src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.short_description: Singleton managing JFR event metadata, registration, serialization and JVM metadata interaction
src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.description:
MetadataRepository is the central singleton responsible for managing Flight Recorder (JFR) metadata for both Java-side and native (JVM) event types. It holds collections of native event types and controls, coordinates registration and unregistration of Java event classes, produces a binary metadata descriptor that is stored in the JVM, and mediates interactions with the native side through JVMSupport/JVM calls and TypeLibrary. The class also manages runtime settings (via SettingsManager), periodic JVM event wiring, and ensures unique chunk timestamps when starting outputs so the downstream parser behaves correctly.

The design centers on a single shared instance (private static final instance) guarded with synchronized methods to serialize modifications and queries that must be consistent with JVM native state. MetadataRepository initializes JVM platform event types at construction (via TypeLibrary and PlatformEventType/Type abstractions), provides APIs to register/unregister Java event classes (including handling of native mirror types), and serializes visible TypeLibrary state to a binary descriptor which is stored in the JVM (JVM.storeMetadataDescriptor). It also tracks transient flags (staleMetadata, unregistered) to minimize unnecessary writes and coordinates with TypeLibrary.clearUnregistered to keep metadata coherent.

Because this class straddles Java-side metadata and native JVM state it contains several non-obvious behaviors: special handling for Java classes that mirror native types (and transfer native field metadata), logic for ensuring unique millisecond timestamps for chunks (awaitEpochMilliShift), interactions with instrumentation and retransform requests when enabling events, and unhideInternalTypes which makes internal-only Types visible and forces a metadata store. Editors must respect the synchronization contracts and the ordering of operations (e.g., storing metadata before setOutput, setting event registered flags before adding to TypeLibrary), as well as native side expectations (JVM.* and JVMSupport.* calls).

key_constructs.reasoning: This is a critical synchronization boundary: it ensures metadata is stored before the JVM emits events into a new output/chunk, enforces timestamp uniqueness via awaitEpochMilliShift, invokes native JVM.setOutput, notifies repository file observers, and handles TypeLibrary cleanup when unregistered flag is set.

key_constructs.name: awaitEpochMilliShift
key_constructs.purpose: Busy-waits (with sleeps) until current epoch milli is different from lastMillis to guarantee unique millisecond timestamps
key_constructs.reasoning: This loop checks JVM.nanosNow and converts to epoch millis then sleeps via HiddenWait.takeNap(1). It is a subtle synchronization mechanism ensuring chunk timestamps differ; modifications risk creating duplicate chunk times.

It avoids unregistering JVM internal types and coordinates with JVM.unregisterStackFilter. Editing logic here affects unloading behavior and interactions with native stack filters.

key_constructs.reasoning: Used to expose otherwise-internal types (e.g., for tooling). It logs unhide operations and calls storeDescriptorInJVM; callers expect the singleton instance to be initialized before this runs to avoid deadlock.

key_constructs.name: flush
key_constructs.purpose: Ensures up-to-date metadata is stored and calls JVM.flush to flush native buffers
key_constructs.reasoning: Public API to ensure that metadata and native state are flushed; it relies on storeDescriptorInJVM if staleMetadata is set.

key_constructs.reasoning: Small wrapper exposing native stack filter registration. Any changes to signature or behavior must remain compatible with native JVM expectations.

src/jdk.hotspot.agent/share/classes/sun/.short_description: Serviceability Agents: enumerate and wrap VM JavaThread structures and provide thread-related queries
src/jdk.hotspot.agent/share/classes/sun/.description:
This file is part of the HotSpot Serviceability Agent (SA). It exists to locate the in-VM global Java thread list, construct Java-side wrapper objects for VM JavaThread instances, and provide utility queries over those thread wrappers. It ties together type information from the TypeDataBase, platform-specific thread PDAccess implementations, and the VirtualConstructor (which maps runtime VM concrete types to SA wrapper classes). The class is used by SA tooling (e.g., jstack, clhsdb, other debugging and inspection utilities) that need to inspect live or core-file JVM state.

Design decisions: Threads uses VM initialization observers to delay DB lookups until the VM is initialized. It resolves the host OS and CPU and selects a JavaThreadPDAccess implementation (several specific platform classes are imported, plus a reflective fallback for linux_<cpu> naming patterns). It populates a VirtualConstructor with mappings from VM type names to wrapper classes so that instantiateWrapperFor can return appropriately-typed wrappers for JavaThread subclasses. Threads wraps a ThreadsList VMObject (which reads the underlying _threads array and _length fields) and exposes operations to get thread wrappers by index, compute the number of threads, and run various thread-centric queries (finding monitor owners, threads pending on a monitor, threads waiting on a monitor, and performing oopsDo on all threads).

Interactions: Threads depends on and must remain consistent with many SA types: VM, TypeDataBase, VMObjectFactory, JavaThread and its subclasses, JavaThreadPDAccess implementations, VirtualConstructor and low-level wrappers like ObjectMonitor and OopHandle. The VirtualConstructor mappings must match VM-internal type names; when the VM introduces new internal JavaThread subclasses, this mapping must be kept in sync (the commit history shows a prior bugfix that added JfrRecorderThread to the mapping).

key_constructs.name: ThreadsList
key_constructs.purpose: VMObject wrapper around the VM-side ThreadsList structure (fields _threads and _length)
key_constructs.reasoning: Encapsulates low-level access to the threads array and length fields; used by Threads to obtain JavaThread addresses and the list length.

key_constructs.name: getJavaThreadAddressAt
key_constructs.purpose: Return the Address of the JavaThread at index i in the VM threads array
key_constructs.reasoning: Performs pointer arithmetic using the VM address size and the _threads pointer; callers expect a raw Address that VirtualConstructor can wrap.

key_constructs.name: length
key_constructs.purpose: Return the length of the ThreadsList (value of _length)
key_constructs.reasoning: Used by callers to bound iterations; returns VM-side integer size (long) and is cast later where needed.

key_constructs.name: Threads
key_constructs.purpose: Primary SA class exposing thread list operations and wrapper construction
key_constructs.reasoning: Constructs a ThreadsList wrapper and provides higher-level operations (getJavaThreadAt, createJavaThreadWrapper, oopsDo, monitor-related queries) used throughout SA tooling.

key_constructs.name: initialize
key_constructs.purpose: Static initialization that resolves type fields, selects platform PDAccess, and configures VirtualConstructor mappings
key_constructs.reasoning: Executed on VM initialization (via observer). Must register all expected VM thread subclass mappings and choose the correct JavaThreadPDAccess for the host OS/CPU.

key_constructs.name: createJavaThreadWrapper
key_constructs.purpose: Instantiate an appropriately-typed JavaThread wrapper for a VM thread Address
key_constructs.reasoning: Defers to VirtualConstructor.instantiateWrapperFor and then sets the thread PDAccess; exceptions are wrapped with a descriptive RuntimeException listing expected VM type names.

key_constructs.name: getJavaThreadAt
key_constructs.purpose: Return a JavaThread wrapper for the i-th thread or null if i out-of-range
key_constructs.reasoning: Bounds-checks against the ThreadsList length and delegates wrapper creation to createJavaThreadWrapper.

key_constructs.name: getNumberOfThreads
key_constructs.purpose: Return number of threads as an int (casts from VM-side long)
key_constructs.reasoning: Provides a convenient integer count for iterations in the SA code; note the cast from long to int.

key_constructs.name: oopsDo
key_constructs.purpose: Call oopsDo on each JavaThread wrapper with a supplied AddressVisitor
key_constructs.reasoning: Used to visit oop references held by threads; it obtains the Threads instance from VM.getVM() rather than relying on instance state, then iterates threads invoking thread.oopsDo.

key_constructs.name: owningThreadFromMonitor
key_constructs.purpose: Two overloads: find the JavaThread owning a monitor by owner id or by ObjectMonitor semantics
key_constructs.reasoning: Encodes logic for anonymous-owned monitors vs explicitly owned monitors; consults LockingMode and uses either stackLocker() or owner() paths, and iterates all threads checking isLockOwned.

key_constructs.name: getPendingThreads
key_constructs.purpose: Return list of JavaThread wrappers that are pending on a specific ObjectMonitor
key_constructs.reasoning: Iterates all threads and compares thread.getCurrentPendingMonitor() with the provided monitor; hides threads that are hiddenFromExternalView.

key_constructs.name: getWaitingThreads
key_constructs.purpose: Return list of JavaThread wrappers that are waiting on a specific ObjectMonitor (via Object.wait)
key_constructs.reasoning: Iterates all threads and compares thread.getCurrentWaitingMonitor() with the provided monitor.

selects platform-specific JavaThreadPDAccess based on VM OS/CPU
creates JavaThread wrappers from raw VM Addresses

pitfalls.consequence: VirtualConstructor.instantiateWrapperFor can fail to resolve the proper wrapper type, causing createJavaThreadWrapper to throw a RuntimeException; SA tools (jstack/clhsdb) may malfunction for VMs with that thread type.
pitfalls.prevention: Keep the mapping set in initialize synchronized with VM-internal type names; if new VM thread types are introduced, ensure mappings are added.

pitfalls.mistake: Changing the platform dispatch logic (OS/CPU checks) or the expected package/class-name conventions used by the reflective fallback
pitfalls.consequence: Threads may fail to find a JavaThreadPDAccess for the running OS/CPU and throw a RuntimeException on VM initialization, preventing SA from functioning on that platform.
pitfalls.prevention: Preserve OS/CPU branch logic and the fallback reflection naming scheme; if modifying, ensure all supported platforms are still covered and add tests on each platform.

pitfalls.mistake: Altering ThreadList field names (_threads, _length) or type names looked up in TypeDataBase without updating the code
pitfalls.consequence: TypeDataBase lookups will fail (NoSuchType) or fields will be incorrect leading to invalid memory reads and crashes in the SA.
pitfalls.prevention: When VM-side structures change, update the TypeDataBase lookups and field names used here; maintain the VM.registerVMInitializedObserver pattern to delay lookups.

pitfalls.mistake: Assuming getNumberOfThreads() never overflows int
pitfalls.consequence: If the VM ever exposes a _length larger than Integer.MAX_VALUE, callers casting to int could truncate and cause silent bugs.
pitfalls.prevention: Be aware getNumberOfThreads casts long to int; if editing code that depends on the maximum number of threads, preserve the cast or update callers accordingly.

src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.short_description: Container managing timed methods for a class and emitting MethodTiming events.
src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.description:
TimedClass is a small concurrency-safe holder for per-class timing state used by the JFR (Java Flight Recorder) tracing subsystem. It maps method ids to TimedMethod instances, exposes operations to add/remove timed methods, mark them published, and produce MethodTiming events from the aggregated timing counters. The class exists to group and manage timing aggregates for all methods belonging to a single Java class and to centralize logic for producing consistent min/avg/max values when emitting a MethodTimingEvent.

Design-wise TimedClass is intentionally simple: a ConcurrentHashMap keyed by method id stores TimedMethod instances. Public operations are add (create-or-get), remove, publish (mark all stored methods as published and write a log entry on the Method), and emit, which reads atomic counters from TimedMethod and calls MethodTimingEvent.commit. The emit method contains non-trivial aggregation logic and sentinel handling to signal missing values when clocks are low-resolution or no samples exist. The class depends on TimedMethod, Method, and jdk.jfr.events.MethodTimingEvent; changes to those types are likely to require coordinated updates here.

This file encapsulates behavior that was recently adjusted in commits described in the commit insights: addressing low-resolution clock behavior (treating zero total time or zero invocations as 'missing' and emitting sentinel values), introducing MISSING sentinel (Long.MIN_VALUE), and ensuring emitted min/avg/max are coherent (average rounding, substituting average when min/max are missing, clamping min to <= average <= max). Because it interacts with event representation and JFR consumers, the emitted semantics (choice of sentinel, average computation, min/max coerce) are part of its observable behavior and must be preserved when editing.

key_constructs.reasoning: Commit history shows this sentinel was introduced to signal 'missing' results to event consumers. Its value and usage are part of the public event representation and should not be changed without coordinating with event schema/consumers.

key_constructs.reasoning: Contains the critical aggregation and emission policy: handles zero-time or zero-invocations as 'missing', computes average with rounding, substitutes average for missing min/max, clamps min/max relative to average, and logs an 'Emitted event' message per method. These behaviors are the core observable semantics and must be preserved.

pitfalls.prevention: Keep the special-case path that emits MISSING sentinels for these cases.

src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.short_description: Record holding atomic timing measurements (invocations/time/min/max) for traced methods.
src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.description:
TimedMethod is a small, concurrency-aware data holder used by the JFR (Java Flight Recorder) tracing subsystem to accumulate per-method timing statistics. It is implemented as a Java record (so fields are final) containing AtomicLong counters for invocation count and accumulated time, AtomicLong sentinels for minimum and maximum durations, a reference to a Method descriptor (from the tracing package), and an AtomicBoolean published flag. The record exists to gather measurements for use by a MethodTiming event and to allow lock-free updates from multiple threads.

Design choices: atomic primitives are used to avoid locks in high-concurrency scenarios. The minimum is initialized to Long.MAX_VALUE and the maximum to Long.MIN_VALUE so that the first real sample will replace the sentinels. The updateMinMax method uses CAS-style loops with weakCompareAndSetVolatile to attempt lock-free updates when a new observed duration exceeds the current maximum or is lower than the current minimum. The method also explicitly ignores zero-duration samples (a guard added per commit notes) to avoid pollution from low-resolution clocks. Because the record fields are final, references to the AtomicLongs/AtomicBoolean are stable and safe to publish.

How it fits: this class is a building block for JFR tracing of method execution times. Other classes in jdk.jfr.internal.tracing (for example the Method descriptor and the code that records/increments invocations and time) interact with TimedMethod: they create instances per method and update its counters from instrumentation points. The published flag is expected to be used by the commit/flush logic that reads the counters and publishes MethodTiming events (not present in this file).

key_constructs.name: TimedMethod
key_constructs.purpose: Record type that holds atomic counters and metadata for a single traced method.
key_constructs.reasoning: Treating TimedMethod as a record makes its fields final and stable; its fields are AtomicLong/AtomicBoolean to allow lock-free concurrent updates from instrumentation sites. An agent editing this file must preserve the semantics of the fields (initial sentinel values for min/max, use of Atomic types) because other tracing code relies on them for correct aggregation and publication.

key_constructs.name: updateMinMax
key_constructs.purpose: Atomically update the stored minimum and maximum durations if the provided duration is a new extreme.
key_constructs.reasoning: This method is the concurrency-sensitive piece: it ignores zero durations (to avoid low-resolution-clock artifacts) and uses CAS loops with weakCompareAndSetVolatile to update AtomicLong minimum/maximum. Editors must respect the control flow (guards, getPlain reads, CAS loop logic) and semantics of weak CAS (may spuriously fail) and the sentinel initialization values (Long.MAX_VALUE and Long.MIN_VALUE).

pitfalls.mistake: Removing the zero-duration guard in updateMinMax or treating duration==0 as meaningful
pitfalls.consequence: Zero samples (from low-resolution clocks) would skew minimum values to zero and corrupt min/max statistics.
pitfalls.prevention: Keep the guard that ignores duration==0 when updating min/max.

pitfalls.mistake: Altering initialization of minimum/maximum AtomicLong sentinels
pitfalls.consequence: If minimum is not initialized to Long.MAX_VALUE or maximum not to Long.MIN_VALUE, the first real sample may not correctly replace the sentinel, causing incorrect reported extremes.
pitfalls.prevention: Preserve sentinel initial values (Long.MAX_VALUE for minimum, Long.MIN_VALUE for maximum).

pitfalls.mistake: Changing CAS loop logic (e.g., swapping weakCompareAndSetVolatile for a non-volatile or non-weak CAS) without understanding semantics
pitfalls.consequence: CAS semantics and memory visibility requirements may be violated leading to lost updates or visibility issues under concurrency.
pitfalls.prevention: Respect current use of getPlain/get and weakCompareAndSetVolatile and ensure any replacement provides equivalent atomicity and visibility guarantees on supported JVMs.

pitfalls.consequence: Platform/JVM differences in VarHandle- or AtomicLong implementation semantics could affect correctness of lock-free updates.
pitfalls.prevention: When editing, consider compatibility and semantics of atomic operations; run concurrency-sensitive tests if behavior is changed.

src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.short_description: Immutable value object representing an amount per time unit and utilities to parse and compare rates
src/jdk.jfr/share/classes/jdk/jfr/intern.description:
This file defines a compact immutable value type (a Java record) named Rate used by the JFR (Java Flight Recorder) internals to model occurrences per time unit. It encapsulates two pieces of data: a long amount and a TimespanUnit denoting the time denominator (e.g., per-second, per-minute). The class provides parsing from textual rate expressions, numeric conversion helpers to convert the stored rate to a common base (nanoseconds and per-second), and a comparison helper to determine which rate is higher. It exists to give other JFR components a single, precise representation for rate-like configuration values and metrics comparisons.

The design uses a Java record to make the data immutable and to provide concise accessors for amount and unit. Parsing is performed by a static factory Rate.of(String) that expects a string with exactly one '/' separator (amount/unit), trims whitespace, resolves the unit via TimespanUnit.fromText(...), and parses the amount as a long. Conversion helpers include a private inNanos() that normalizes the amount to a per-nanosecond basis (as a double) and a public perSecond() that multiplies that normalized value by 1e9 to produce occurrences per second. The isHigher(Rate) method relies on inNanos() for comparisons so comparisons are unit-agnostic.

Because this file references TimespanUnit and relies on its semantics (notably a nanos field and a fromText factory), maintainers editing this file must respect the contract of TimespanUnit (valid text forms, nanos non-zero positive values). This file is small and focused on representation and conversion; other JFR components will consume Rate objects for configuration parsing and runtime comparisons, so changes here can affect parsing behavior, comparisons, and numeric conversions across the JFR module.

test/jdk/jdk/jfr/event/profiling/TestCPU.short_description: JTReg test verifying JFR CPUTimeSample event throttling using thread CPU-time measurements.
test/jdk/jdk/jfr/event/profiling/TestCPU.description:
This is a JTReg test class that validates the throttling behavior of the JFR CPUTimeSample event. It exists to ensure that different throttle configurations produce expected sampling rates in terms of CPU-time consumed by the current thread. Instead of relying on wall-clock time, the test measures thread CPU-time (via the ThreadMXBean) and counts emitted CPUTimeSample events in a Recording. This design makes the test resilient to external system load and scheduling variability and focuses validation on how JFR throttles sampling relative to CPU consumption.

The test runs three independent checks: zero-per-second throttling (expecting no events), a small rate based on core count (expecting a very low count), and a fine-grained period throttle (expecting ~100 samples/sec). It constructs a Recording, enables EventNames.CPUTimeSample with different "throttle" options, performs CPU work on the current thread (wasteCPU), stops the recording, then collects and filters events by the current thread name. The event counting and CPU-time measurement are combined into an EventCount record whose rate() returns samples per CPU-second. The class uses test harness utilities (jdk.test.lib.Asserts and jdk.test.lib.jfr.Events/EventNames), so it must run under the JTReg harness (or an equivalent test runtime that provides those libs).

Key design decisions: (1) Use of ThreadMXBean.getCurrentThreadCpuTime() to compute elapsed CPU-time (not wall-clock), making the test wall-clock independent; (2) Counting events filtered by the current thread name to attribute samples to the busy thread; (3) Explicit throttle strings passed to recording.enable(...).with("throttle", throttle), relying on JFR's accepted throttle formats (e.g., "0/s", "10ms", "N/s"). Historical commit notes indicate this file was adjusted to measure CPU-time rather than wall-clock and the period assertion lower bound was relaxed (to 75) to improve resilience. The test is annotated with @requires vm.hasJFR & os.family == "linux", so it will only execute in environments that satisfy those conditions.

test/jdk/jdk/jfr/event/profiling/TestCPU.short_description: jtreg test that verifies CPUTimeSample and ExecutionSample JFR events under specific timing attributes
test/jdk/jdk/jfr/event/profiling/TestCPU.description:
This file is a jtreg integration test targeting Java Flight Recorder (JFR) profiling events. Its goal is to exercise two JFR event types (CPUTimeSample and ExecutionSample) with specific event attribute values to provoke JVM behavior related to OS sleep/throttling thresholds. The test runs four scenarios combining the two event types with attribute values that are intended to trigger the JVM's internal threshold logic (notably the 1000 ms naked_short_sleep threshold referenced in comments).

The test uses RecordingStream to enable and listen for events, and it uses a helper RecurseThread from the test library to produce call stacks (depth 50). When an event is observed, the event handler calls t.quit() on the helper thread and closes the RecordingStream, allowing the test to finish. The test is time- and scheduling-sensitive and is explicitly constrained to run only when the VM has JFR and the OS family is Linux (see jtreg annotations). It also depends on test libraries under /test/lib (EventNames and RecurseThread) and requests the jdk.jfr.internal module in the annotation block.

src/jdk.zipfs/share/classes/module-info..short_description: Java module descriptor declaring the jdk.zipfs module and its FileSystemProvider service provider
src/jdk.zipfs/share/classes/module-info..description:
This file is the Java module descriptor (module-info.java) for the jdk.zipfs module. Its principal purpose is to declare the module name (jdk.zipfs) and to register the ZIP file system provider implementation (jdk.nio.zipfs.ZipFileSystemProvider) as a service provider for the java.nio.file.spi.FileSystemProvider service. The file also contains an extensive Javadoc block that documents the ZIP file system provider's semantics, supported provider properties, POSIX attribute behavior, and examples — this documentation describes the runtime contract consumers rely on.

Why it exists: the module declaration is required by the Java Platform Module System to make the module known to the module graph at compile-time and run-time. The provides clause is the mechanism by which this module advertises its service implementation so that java.nio.file.FileSystems and other consumers can locate the ZIP file system provider via the standard service-loading mechanisms. This descriptor therefore affects module resolution, service discovery, and the public API surface of the runtime image produced by the build.

How it fits with the larger system: other parts of the JDK (notably the java.nio.file APIs and the FileSystems.newFileSystem factory) rely on the presence of this module and the registered provider to create ZIP/JAR-backed file systems. The descriptor references fully-qualified names (the provider class and the service interface) that must be present and accessible in the module's compiled output. Changes to this file can alter module visibility, service loading behavior, and the set of providers available at runtime, and so they interact with build, packaging, and tests that exercise ZIP filesystem functionality.

src/java.base/share/classes/java/io/Rand.short_description: Public java.io.RandomAccessFile implementation providing random-access I/O and a FileChannel.
src/java.base/share/classes/java/io/Rand.description:
This file implements java.io.RandomAccessFile: the public API for random-access file I/O in the JDK. It provides constructors to open a file (by path or File), mode-string parsing for "r", "rw", "rws", and "rwd", low-level open semantics via a native open0, read and write primitives (with bulk-read/write variants), a lazily-created associated FileChannel (FileChannelImpl.open), and integration with FileDescriptor cleanup. The class exists to provide a legacy, well-known API that interoperates with NIO FileChannel: the FileChannel returned is kept in sync with this object's file pointer and file length changes.

Design decisions visible in the source: the class keeps a FileDescriptor fd and a volatile FileChannel channel and uses double-checked locking to lazily create the channel via FileChannelImpl.open (passing this as the attachment). There are native methods (open0, read0, readBytes0, etc.) that implement the low-level reads/writes; Java-side wrappers add behavior such as Java Flight Recorder (JFR) tracing. JFR tracing is guarded by a static boolean jfrTracing and event enablement checks; trace wrappers capture a timestamp and call FileReadEvent.offer / FileWriteEvent.offer in finally blocks to emit telemetry. The constructors attach the RandomAccessFile to the FileDescriptor and register a FileCleanable to ensure FD cleanup if the object is abandoned. Mode-parsing enforces exact allowed strings and maps them to internal O_* flags including a temporary-open flag used when openAndDelete is specified.

src/java.base/share/classes/java/securit.short_description: A Java record representing PEM (RFC 7468) data with type, Base64 content, and optional leading non‑PEM bytes.
src/java.base/share/classes/java/securit.description:
PEMRecord is a public Java record (since JDK 25, marked as a preview API) that models a single PEM block: a type identifier (the value that appears in PEM header/footer), the Base64-encoded content, and any bytes that preceded the PEM block during decoding (leadingData). It exists to provide a lightweight, immutable holder for PEM data in cases where the data should not or cannot be converted into a specific cryptographic object; PEMDecoder and PEMEncoder use this representation when a DEREncodable object is not appropriate. The record implements DEREncodable so it can participate in APIs expecting a DEREncodable representation.

Design choices visible in the file: the record is intentionally minimal and does not perform extensive validation — it only enforces non-null for type and content and rejects values that obviously contain PEM syntax labels (strings starting with '-' or the prefixes "BEGIN " or "END "). leadingData is intentionally not defensively copied and may be null; this is documented and part of the API contract. The toString method delegates to an internal helper (sun.security.util.Pem.pemEncoded) to produce the canonical PEM multi-line string; that means string rendering/formatting is delegated to internal utilities rather than implemented here.

Because the record is part of java.base and is annotated with a PreviewFeature, maintainers and editing agents must respect preview API semantics (annotation usage) and the public API surface expectations. The class imports a jdk.internal.javac.PreviewFeature (internal API for preview annotation) and uses sun.security.util.Pem (JDK-internal utility) for encoding; edits should consider module boundaries, access to internal packages, and the implications for API compatibility and runtime access within the JDK itself.

src/java.base/share/classes/java/securit.short_description: Immutable, thread-safe PEM data decoder that maps PEM types to Java crypto objects.
src/java.base/share/classes/java/securit.description:
PEMDecoder is a final, immutable, thread-safe utility in java.security that decodes PEM (textual Base64) encoded security objects (keys, certificates, CRLs, encrypted private keys, and generic PEMRecords) into concrete Java cryptographic types. It centralizes decoding logic for multiple PEM types (PUBLIC KEY, PRIVATE KEY, ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY, CERTIFICATE, CRL, RSA PRIVATE KEY, and fallback to generic PEMRecord). The class exists to provide a single public API for consumers to decode PEM data from Strings or InputStreams and to optionally constrain the decoding to factory implementations from a specific Provider and/or a decryption password.

Design and purpose: the class abstracts parsing/interpretation of PEM payloads (using the internal sun.security.util.Pem helper) and then maps that raw data to Java objects using standard JCA/JCE mechanisms: KeyFactory, CertificateFactory, EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo, and KeySpec conversions. It handles PKCS#8 v1/v2 variants (PKCS8Key, potential embedded public key bytes), RSA CRT keys, and X.509 certificates/CRLs. The decoder uses Base64 MIME decoding and treats String inputs as UTF-8. It wraps underlying GeneralSecurityException/IOExceptions into IllegalArgumentException for most decoding failures (except declared IO exceptions on stream-based public APIs). The class is annotated with @PreviewFeature(PEM_API) indicating this API is a preview, and it uses internal sun.* classes (PKCS8Key, RSAPrivateCrtKeyImpl, Pem) for parsing/compatibility with existing internal implementations.

How it fits: this is the canonical JDK-side implementation for decoding PEM-encoded artifacts into runtime objects used by the rest of the platform and potential user code. Other parts of the platform that need to convert PEM strings/files into PrivateKey/PublicKey/Certificate objects should call this API. It depends on internal parsing utilities (sun.security.util.Pem) and on standard factory mechanics (KeyFactory, CertificateFactory, EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo), and it forwards provider selection when configured via withFactory(provider).
